Data centers constructed for hyperscalers to lease are off-balance sheet during construction. Hyperscalers, in partnership with private credit, create Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) to finance data center developments. These SPVs are considered "variable interest entities" (VIE) for accounting purposes because as the sole tenant of the data center, hyperscalers have more exposure to and influence on the SPV than their minority equity ownership and voting rights would suggest.

VIE structures became increasingly common and used to circumvent consolidation in the late '90s and early '00s, just before the dot com bubble burst and around the time of the massive fiber overbuild. In response, consolidation accounting was updated so that VIEs would be consolidated by the SPV's "primary beneficiary". For a hyperscaler to be considered the primary beneficiary of a lease SPV, it must have both (1) the power to direct the most economically significant activities and (2) the obligation to absorb the entity's losses or the right to receive the entity's economic benefits.

Martin Casado and Steven Sinofsky on why AI is turning engineering problems into capital problems:

"Right now, if I give 20 people a billion dollars, they can actually use it usefully... We've never been like that before."

"This is like a law of physics where our early intuition, which is like all problems are engineering problems, starts to change... It changes the nature of capital versus innovation versus competition versus defensibility."

"Mad Men goes through the scenario where the computer shows up at the advertising agency... They couldn't figure out what to do, but they were excited that they had the capital to acquire one, and it made them look like they knew what they were doing."

WHO PAYS FOR THE DAM WATER?

Everyone is throwing around numbers on data center water use vs. golf courses, so we went back to the sources.

Golf: 1.63M acre-ft, or 531B gallons (GCSAA, 2024)
Data centers: 17.4B gallons direct, 211B gallons indirect (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2023)

So golf uses 30x more water than data centers at the site: 531B vs. 17.4B.

Add the water attributed to generating the necessary electricity and the gap collapses to 2.3x: 531B vs. 228B.

How to treat hydropower in this equation is where things get very weird -->

LBNL counts evaporation from hydro reservoirs as water consumed generating electricity. Fair enough. But reservoirs often serve several purposes, so you have to decide how much of that evaporation actually belongs to power.

The methodology uses a surprisingly binary rule. If hydropower is listed as a reservoir's primary purpose in the federal National Inventory of Dams, electricity gets charged 100% of the evaporation. If hydro is secondary, it gets zero.

This matters a lot: Hydro supplies only ~5.5% of U.S. electricity, but reservoir evaporation accounts for roughly 60% of the water LBNL attributes to data centers' electricity use.

Libby Dam in Montana is a good example of how strange this can get.

The federal database lists its primary purpose as hydropower, so electricity gets charged with 100% of Lake Koocanusa's evaporation.

But the Army Corps operates Libby for flood-risk management and hydropower, along with recreation, fish and wildlife and water quality. Nearly 5 million acre-ft of the reservoir is allocated to flood storage.

Grand Coulee shows the problem in reverse. It's the largest hydropower complex in the U.S. and can generate ~21 TWh a year. But the federal database lists its primary purpose as flood-risk reduction, so its reservoir evaporation isn't charged to hydropower at all. It also irrigates ~680,000 acres.

There isn't one obvious answer here. But that's the problem with a 100-or-zero rule for multipurpose reservoirs. A huge amount of water can move on or off electricity's tab based on which purpose occupies one field in a federal database.

Use USGS/NLR power-sector estimates that exclude hydro evaporation and indirect data center water use falls from 211B gallons to roughly 83B.

Suddenly golf isn't using 2.3x as much water as data centers. It's closer to 5x.

Now, looking forward:

Golf water use is down 31% since 2005 and another 3.2% since 2020. Data center power demand obviously isn't down. LBNL now estimates 649 TWh of annual electricity consumption in 2030, equivalent to ~74 GW running continuously, versus ~20 GW in 2023.

Direct data center water use was only 17.4B gallons in 2023. Even if water intensity doesn't improve at all, 3.7x the power demand gets you to ~64B gallons in 2030. Golf is at 531B today.

And the direct data center estimate is almost certainly too high. More than half of new hyperscale builds are moving to closed-loop cooling (90%+ less water use), so direct water use should grow much more slowly than power demand.

For a deliberately conservative comparison, though, assume no improvement at all. Scale today's entire direct + electricity footprint with demand, but leave out hydro reservoir evaporation, and you get roughly 370B gallons in 2030.

Still ~30% below golf.

(Count hydro evaporation, though, and data centers pass golf before 2030.

Turns out the delta mostly comes down to who pays for the dam water.)
